historical_record.description: The newly founded Kinmon Gakuen (Golden Gate Institute) held its Japanese language school in a rented earlier building on this site, under its first principal Masayoshi Kamada.
After years of fundraising, the Kinmon Gakuen Foundation bought the parcel for $24,000 to build a purpose-built school.
Ground was broken for the new Kinmon Gakuen building, after the school's earlier building on the site had been demolished.

Purpose-built premises for the Kinmon Gakuen, or Golden Gate School, a Japanese language school that had first enrolled pupils in 1911 and taught ikebana, Japanese instruments and etiquette alongside the language.

The Mediterranean Revival school building, designed by William C. Hays and built for $46,545 with money raised by the Issei community and a $44,500 Anglo California Bank loan, was dedicated; classes began soon after.
Prince and Princess Takamatsu of Japan visited classes at the school.
Prince and Princess Kaya of Japan visited the school.
A projection (moving-picture) booth was built for the school auditorium, later home to the weekend Japanese film nights of the 1950s and 60s.
One of the places in the city where San Francisco's Japanese community was ordered to register and report for processing in 1942 before wartime removal.

The Booker T. Washington Community Service Center leased this building in 1942 and stayed until 1952. It had housed the Kinmon Gakuen Japanese language school until the incarceration of the city's Japanese American population that year.

The Booker T. Washington Community Service Center opened a Red Cross center for Black San Franciscans in the building, offering public-health services such as chest X-rays during a tuberculosis outbreak.

The Booker T. Washington Center moved into the building during the war and, with the American Friends Service Committee, ran a men's hostel here for those returning from the internment camps; the language school had reopened by 1949.
Kinmon Gakuen moved back into its building once the Booker T. Washington center had left, reopening here with 88 pupils.
The school's teachers began adult English classes, after weekend American citizenship classes started on its return.
Japan's Crown Prince Akihito and the Crown Princess visited the school, drawing thousands into the street.
The Redevelopment Agency photographed the property.
Nihonmachi Little Friends, a bilingual Japanese childcare center, leased the auditorium, and new restrooms, a kitchen and an office were put in.
Aluminium-sash windows were fitted within existing window openings.
More aluminium windows replaced original windows in the classrooms.
Recorded in the city's 2009 survey of Japantown as the Kinmon Gakuen building, by then also home to Nihonmachi Little Friends, and taken as representative of the neighborhood's school buildings.
Nihonmachi Little Friends left the building for a permanent home in the historic Japanese YWCA on Sutter Street.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 288, Kinmon Gakuen.

unknowns: The city's Japantown context statement has the Kinmon Gakuen in its purpose-built premises here by 1926; the assessor's roll and Planning's historic resource survey both record 1924.
The school is said to have reopened here by 1949, though it also reopened in rented space elsewhere and returned only in May 1952.

notable_residents.name: Robert B. Flippin
notable_residents.detail: Robert B. Flippin, NAACP treasurer, journalist and in 1943 a San Francisco Housing Authority appointee, was executive director of the Booker T. Washington Community Service Center while it was based here.

notable_residents.name: Koshi Suzuki
notable_residents.detail: Koshi Suzuki was principal of Kinmon Gakuen until his death, apart from the wartime closure, and led its postwar revival.
